title: Getting to Yes
author: Roger Fisher & William Ury
tagline: Negotiating agreement without giving in — the Harvard method: principled negotiation on the merits.
oneLiner: Don't bargain over positions: separate people from problems, focus on interests, invent options, insist on objective criteria — and know your BATNA.
bigIdea: The Harvard Negotiation Project's field manual — the most influential negotiation book ever written — replaces the two broken defaults (HARD bargaining: contest of wills that damages relationships; SOFT bargaining: concessions that produce resentful losers) with PRINCIPLED NEGOTIATION on four legs: SEPARATE THE PEOPLE FROM THE PROBLEM (be soft on humans, hard on merits — negotiators are people first: egos, emotions, perceptions all in the room), focus on INTERESTS, NOT POSITIONS (positions are what people say they want; interests are WHY — and opposing positions regularly hide compatible interests), INVENT OPTIONS FOR MUTUAL GAIN (separate inventing from deciding; expand the pie before dividing it), and insist on OBJECTIVE CRITERIA (market value, precedent, law, expert standards — so outcomes reflect merit, not stubbornness). The power tool: BATNA — Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — the true measure of negotiating power and the shield against both bad deals and bullies.
quotes: Any method of negotiation may be fairly judged by three criteria: it should produce a wise agreement... it should be efficient... and it should improve or at least not damage the relationship.
The reason you negotiate is to produce something better than the results you can obtain without negotiating.
Separate the people from the problem.

lessons.title: Don't Bargain Over Positions: The Orange and the Library Window
lessons.chapter: Chapters 1–3: The Problem / The Method's First Two Principles
lessons.summary: Positional bargaining's anatomy: each side stakes a position, defends it as ego attaches, concedes grudgingly — producing agreements that are unwise (mechanical splitting rather than merit), inefficient (the concession dance takes forever), and relationship-damaging (a contest of wills leaves a loser). The first two repairs: SEPARATE PEOPLE FROM PROBLEM — attack the issue side-by-side rather than each other face-to-face: handle PERCEPTIONS (see their view from inside; discuss perceptions explicitly), EMOTIONS (recognize and legitimize them; allow steam-venting without reacting), and COMMUNICATION (listen actively, speak about yourself not about them — 'we feel discriminated against' beats 'you broke your word'). Then INTERESTS, NOT POSITIONS: behind every stated position live the needs, fears, and desires that produced it — and while positions clash by construction, interests overlap surprisingly often; the excavation tools: ask WHY (what need does their position serve?) and WHY NOT (what interest blocks what you propose?) — remembering the most powerful interests are basic human needs: security, recognition, control, belonging.
lessons.example: The book's two teaching fables: the sisters quarreling over one ORANGE — compromising by halving it, one discarding her peel (she wanted fruit for eating), the other discarding her fruit (she wanted peel for baking): positions ('the orange is mine') perfectly incompatible; interests perfectly compatible — the whole orange available to each, lost to positional habit. And the library WINDOW: two readers deadlocked — open versus closed — until the librarian asks WHY: one wants fresh air, one fears the draft; she opens a window in the NEXT room: both interests served by an option neither position contained.
lessons.action: For your live negotiation: write their position, then excavate — three WHYs beneath it (what needs produce this demand?) and three beneath your own. Look for the orange: which of your interests are actually compatible? And separate one people-problem from the merits this week: name the emotion explicitly, then return, side-by-side, to the issue.

lessons.title: Invent Options for Mutual Gain: Grow the Pie Before Cutting It
lessons.chapter: Chapter 4: Invent Options for Mutual Gain
lessons.summary: The creative leg. Four obstacles kill option-generation: PREMATURE JUDGMENT (the critic strangling the inventor mid-sentence), searching for THE SINGLE ANSWER (narrowing before exploring), the FIXED-PIE assumption (his gain must be my loss), and 'THEIR problem is theirs' (solving only your side of the equation produces proposals they can't accept). The repairs: SEPARATE INVENTING FROM DECIDING (the brainstorm rule — wild options welcomed, criticism scheduled for later; ideally invent WITH the other side: joint sessions transform adversaries into co-authors), BROADEN the options (the circle chart: cycle between the problem, diagnosis, approaches, and specific actions; examine the issue through different experts' eyes — how would a banker, engineer, psychologist slice this?), hunt for MUTUAL GAIN (shared interests are latent in every negotiation — and DIFFERENCES are the raw material of trade: different valuations, timelines, risk appetites, and forecasts let each side give what's cheap to them and precious to the other), and make their decision EASY (draft the 'yesable proposition': the offer they can accept in one word, with justifications they can carry to their own constituents).
lessons.example: The Camp David masterclass anchors the chapter: Egypt demanded the Sinai's return (sovereignty position); Israel demanded to keep portions (security position) — irreconcilable AS POSITIONS. The interests beneath: Egypt's was sovereignty's symbol (the flag, the map, the pride); Israel's was security (no Egyptian tanks at the border). The invented option contained in neither position: FULL Egyptian sovereignty over a DEMILITARIZED Sinai — flag returned, tanks banned; both interests whole, 1979's treaty signed on the design. The differences-as-material principle runs through Fisher and Ury's smaller cases identically: the seller needing cash NOW and the buyer flush next quarter don't have a conflict — they have the raw material of an installment structure.
lessons.action: Schedule a pure inventing session for your negotiation — thirty minutes, criticism banned, quantity targeted (twenty options minimum, wild ones included); invite the other side if the relationship permits. Then mine the differences deliberately: list where your valuations, timelines, and risk appetites DIVERGE — each divergence is a trade waiting to be structured. Close by drafting the yesable proposition.

lessons.title: Insist on Objective Criteria: Merit as the Referee
lessons.chapter: Chapter 5: Insist on Using Objective Criteria
lessons.summary: The fourth leg dissolves the contest of wills: when interests genuinely conflict (price, deadlines, terms), refuse to settle by stubbornness — insist the outcome rest on OBJECTIVE CRITERIA: market value, replacement cost, precedent, professional standards, law, expert opinion, efficiency, reciprocity ('what a court would decide', 'what others in your position have accepted'). The method's three practices: FRAME each issue as a joint search for criteria ('what's the theory behind that figure? how would we know what's fair here?'), REASON AND BE OPEN TO REASON about which standards apply and how (principled negotiation is not a fancier way to be rigid — the willingness to be persuaded by better criteria IS the credential that earns the other side's), and NEVER YIELD TO PRESSURE — only to principle ('as pressure rises, respond by inviting them to the merits: 'I don't work on the basis of threats — let's look at the standard''). The elegant addition: FAIR PROCEDURES when standards can't decide — the ancient cake-cutting protocol (one cuts, the other chooses) scaled to term-drafting, turn-taking, and third-party arbitration.
lessons.example: The chapter's set-piece is the insurance adjuster: a totaled car, the adjuster's opening offer delivered as verdict — met not with a counter-position but with criteria questions: 'how did you compute that? what would a replacement actually cost at local dealers? what does the blue book say for this trim and mileage?' — each question moving the negotiation from wills (where the adjuster holds the power) to standards (where the facts do); the settlement lands near the documented replacement figure, without a single positional clash. Fisher and Ury's landlord vignette mirrors it: the rent negotiation transformed by 'what are comparable units renting for?' — the standard doing the arguing the tenant's assertiveness never could.
lessons.action: Before your negotiation, research three applicable standards (market comparables, precedent, expert benchmarks) — arrive as the best-informed person on the MERITS in the room. Frame every contested number as a criteria question ('help me understand the basis'). And pre-script your pressure response: 'I don't respond to pressure — I respond to reasons; which standard supports that?'

lessons.title: BATNA: The Power Behind Every Word
lessons.chapter: Chapters 6–8: What If They're More Powerful / Won't Play / Use Dirty Tricks
lessons.summary: The book's most exported concept: your negotiating power is not resources, rank, or nerve — it's your BATNA (Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement): what you'll actually do if no deal happens. The method: DEVELOP it actively (invent alternatives, improve the best one, and know it precisely — the vague 'I'll find something' produces vague courage), MEASURE every proposal against it (the only true test of any offer — protecting you simultaneously from accepting too little and from rejecting what you can't beat), CONSIDER THEIRS (their eagerness is legible in their alternatives), and — the power inversion — the better your BATNA, the more power radiates through every sentence without a threat being spoken. The defensive chapters complete the kit: against opponents who WON'T play, use NEGOTIATION JUJITSU (don't push back — invite critique of your ideas, recast attacks on you as attacks on the problem, ask questions and let silence work) or the ONE-TEXT procedure (a mediator's single draft, iterated by both sides' criticism); against DIRTY TRICKS (deliberate deception, phony authority, good-cop routines, extreme anchors), the meta-move: NAME the tactic explicitly and negotiate the RULES OF THE GAME itself — tricks, recognized aloud, mostly die of exposure.
lessons.example: The BATNA parable Fisher and Ury deploy: the small-town homeowner negotiating with the only buyer in sight versus the same homeowner holding a second written offer — identical house, identical skills, transformed power: the alternative, not the assertiveness, changed every number in the room. The jujitsu exhibit: the negotiator whose response to an attack ('your proposal is ridiculous') is not defense but invitation — 'what specifically concerns you about it? how would you improve it?' — converting the attacker, sentence by sentence, into a co-editor. And the tricks chapter's rule proves itself daily in car showrooms everywhere: 'I notice we're doing good-cop/bad-cop — shall we drop that and talk standards?' ends the theater faster than any counter-performance.
lessons.action: Before ANY significant negotiation: write your BATNA concretely, spend one hour improving it (one more alternative developed changes your voice), estimate theirs, and set your walk-away against the analysis. In the room: measure every offer against the BATNA, not against your hopes. And when a tactic appears — name it, pleasantly, and propose negotiating the rules.

lessons.title: People Problems: Separate the Relationship From the Issue
lessons.summary: The Harvard method's first move is often ignored: every negotiation has two layers — the substance (what we're arguing about) and the relationship (how we feel about each other). Skilled negotiators separate them: be soft on the people, hard on the problem. When emotions run high, the relationship layer poisons the substance layer — so address it first: acknowledge feelings, listen actively, and build rapport before tackling the issue. Attacking the person while negotiating the problem is the fastest way to lose both. The person who treats their counterpart with respect while pushing hard on the numbers wins the deal AND keeps the relationship.
lessons.example: Fisher and Ury describe negotiations where the same terms were accepted or rejected purely based on how the other party was treated — a boss who felt listened to accepted a plan he had earlier rejected, because the issue hadn't changed; the relationship had.
lessons.action: In your next difficult conversation, spend the first two minutes acknowledging the other person's perspective and feelings before raising your own position at all.

lessons.title: Invent Options for Mutual Gain: The Brainstorm Before the Battle
lessons.summary: Most negotiators arrive with one position and fight for it — missing the entire space of solutions that could satisfy both sides. The Harvard method: before deciding, generate options — brainstorm multiple ways to meet everyone's core interests, separating idea generation from evaluation (the classic brainstorming rules). The famous 'orange' example: two people fighting over one orange each need it for different reasons — one for juice, one for the peel — so splitting it in half satisfies neither fully. The creative option (one takes the juice, one takes the peel) satisfies both. Options turn negotiation from zero-sum combat into joint problem-solving.
lessons.example: Fisher and Ury's classic: two sisters fighting over an orange — the one who just wanted the peel to bake and the one who wanted juice. Cutting it in half was 'fair' and useless; giving one the whole peel and the other the whole fruit made both happy.
lessons.action: Before your next negotiation, write at least 5 possible options that could satisfy both sides' real interests — then bring them to the table as a menu, not a position.

actionPlan: Excavate interests: three WHYs beneath their position and yours.
Hold the inventing session — twenty options, judgment suspended.
Arm yourself with three objective standards; yield to principle, never pressure.
Write and improve your BATNA; measure every offer against it.
Name tactics aloud; negotiate the rules when the game turns dirty.
caveat: Principled negotiation assumes the other side is also trying to reach yes. When the counterparty wants the deal dead — a hostile acquirer, a rival blocking your merger — 'focus on interests' becomes a stalling tactic. Quaker's interest-based deal for Snapple felt right to both sides at the table and destroyed value anyway, because the real conflict was outside the room. Sometimes the smartest negotiation is refusing to enter it.
